describe the investment constraints of liquidity, time horizon, tax concerns, legal and regulatory factors, and unique circumstances and their implications for the choice of portfolio assets In the following sections, we analyze five major types of constraints on portfolio selection: liquidity, time horizon, tax concerns, legal and regulatory factors, and unique circumstances. Liquidity Requirements The IPS should state what the likely requirements are to withdraw funds from the portfolio. Examples for an individual investor would be outlays for covering healthcare payments or tuition fees. For institutions, it could be spending rules and requirements for endowment funds, the existence of claims coming due in the case of property and casualty insurance, or benefit payments for pension funds and life insurance companies. When the client does have such a requirement, the manager should allocate part of the portfolio to cover the liability. This part of the portfolio will be invested in assets that are liquid—that is, easily converted to cash—and have low risk when the liquidity need is actually present (e.g., a bond maturing at the time when private education expenses will be incurred), so that their value is known with reasonable certainty. For example, the asset allocation in the insurance portfolios of US insurer Progressive Corporation (see Exhibit 3) shows a large allocation to fixed-income investments (called “Fixed maturities” by the company), some of which are either highly liquid or have a short maturity. These investments enable the company, in the case of automobile insurance, to pay claims for which the timing is unpredictable. IPS Constraints                                                                           171 Exhibit 3: Asset Allocation of Progressive Corporation Fixed maturities, 76.9% Short-term investments, 10.4% Common equities, 10.2% Nonredeemable preferred stocks, 2.5% Source: Progressive Corporation, 2018 Second Quarter Report. Time Horizon The IPS should state the time horizon over which the investor is investing. It may be the period over which the portfolio is accumulating before any assets need to be withdrawn; it could also be the period until the client’s circumstances are likely to change. For example, a 55-year-old pension plan investor hoping to retire at age 65 has a 10-year horizon. The portfolio may not be liquidated at age 65, but its structure may need to change, for example, as the investor begins to draw an income from the fund. The time horizon of the investor will affect the nature of investments used in the portfolio. Illiquid or risky investments may be unsuitable for an investor with a short time horizon because the investor may not have enough time to recover from investment losses, for example. Such investments, however, may be suitable for an investor with a longer horizon, especially if the risky investments are expected to have higher returns. EXAMPLE 5 Investment Time Horizon 1. Frank Johnson is investing for retirement and has a 20-year horizon. He has an average risk tolerance. Which investment is likely to be the least suitable for a major allocation in Johnson’s portfolio? A. Listed equities B. Private equity C. US Treasury bills Solution: C is correct. With a 20-year horizon and average risk tolerance, Johnson can accept the additional risk of listed equities and private equity compared with US Treasury bills. 2. Al Smith has to pay a large tax bill in six months and wants to invest the money in the meantime. Which investment is likely to be the least suitable for a major allocation in Smith’s portfolio? A. Listed equities B. Private equity C. US Treasury bills Solution: B is correct. Private equity is risky, has no public market, and is the least liquid among the assets mentioned. Tax Concerns Tax status varies among investors. Some investors will be subject to taxation on investment returns and some will not. For example, in many countries, returns to pension funds are exempt from tax. Some investors will face a different tax rate on income (dividends and interest payments) than they do on capital gains (associated with increases in asset prices). Typically, when there is a differential, income is taxed more highly than gains. Gains may be subject to a lower tax rate, or part or all of the gain may be exempt from taxation. Furthermore, income may be taxed as it is earned, whereas gains may be taxed when they are realized. Hence, in such cases there is a time value of money benefit in the deferment of taxation of gains relative to income. In many cases, the portfolio should reflect the tax status of the client. For exam- ple, a taxable investor may wish to hold a portfolio that emphasizes capital gains and receives little income. A taxable investor based in the United States is also likely to consider including US municipal bonds (“munis”) in his portfolio because interest income from munis, unlike from Treasuries and corporate bonds, is exempt from taxes. A tax-exempt investor, such as a pension fund, will be relatively indifferent to the form of returns. Legal and Regulatory Factors The IPS should state any legal and regulatory restrictions that constrain how the portfolio is invested. In some countries, such institutional investors as pension funds are subject to restrictions on portfolio composition. For example, there may be a limit on the pro- portion of equities or other risky assets in the portfolio or on the proportion of the portfolio that may be invested overseas. The United States has no limits on pension fund asset allocation, but some countries do, examples of which are shown in Exhibit 4. Pension funds also often face restrictions on the percentage of assets that can be invested in securities issued by the plan sponsor, so called self-investment limits. When an individual has access to material nonpublic information about a particular security, this situation may also form a constraint. For example, the directors of a public company may need to refrain from trading the company’s stock at certain points of the year before financial results are published. The IPS should note this constraint so that the portfolio manager does not inadvertently trade the stock on the client’s behalf. Unique Circumstances and ESG Considerations This section of the IPS should cover any other aspect of the client’s circumstances, including beliefs and values, that is likely to have a material impact on portfolio com- position. A client may have considerations derived from her faith or moral values that could constrain investment choices. For instance, an investor seeking compliance with Shari’a (the Islamic law) will avoid investing in businesses and financial instruments inconsistent with Shari’a, such as casinos and bonds, because Shari’a prohibits gambling and lending money on interest. Similarly, an investor may wish to avoid investments that he believes are inconsistent with his faith. Charitable and pension fund investors may have constituencies that want to express their values in an investment portfolio. Whether rooted in religious beliefs or not, a client may have personal objections to certain products (e.g., weapons, tobacco, gambling) or practices (e.g., environmental impact of business activities, human impact of government policies, labor standards), which could lead to the exclusion of certain companies, countries, or types of secu- rities (e.g., interest-bearing debt) from the investable universe as well as the client’s benchmark. Investing in accordance with such considerations is referred to as socially responsible investing (SRI). Specific ESG investment approaches can be classified in a variety of ways, and the investment community lacks clear consensus on terminology. We define six generic ESG investment approaches: ■    Negative screening: Excluding companies or sectors based on business activi- ties or environmental or social concerns; ■    Positive screening: Including sectors or companies based on specific ESG criteria, typically ESG performance relative to industry peers; ■    ESG integration: Systematic consideration of material ESG factors in asset allocation, security selection, and portfolio construction decisions; ■    Thematic investing: Investing in themes or assets related to ESG factors; ■    Engagement/active ownership: Using shareholder power to influence cor- porate behavior to achieve targeted ESG objectives along with financial returns; and ■    Impact investing: Investments made with the intention to generate positive, measurable social and environmental impact alongside a financial return. These ESG investment approaches may impact a portfolio manager’s investment universe and may also require the investment management firm to put in place a process to systematically incorporate ESG factors into the investment process. For example, an employee of a public company whose labor income and retirement income provision are reliant on that company, and who may have substantial investment exposure to the company through employee share options and stock holdings, may decide that his portfolio should not invest additional amounts in that stock. An entrepreneur may be reluctant to see her portfolio invested in the shares of competing businesses or in any business that has risk exposures aligned with her entrepreneurial venture. A client’s income may rely on a particular industry or asset class. Appropriate diversification requires that industry or asset class to be de-emphasized in the cli- ent’s investments. 1: ## What ethics is
Ethics = principles that guide good choices. Situational influences (pressure, incentives, peers) often push people off course more than they realize.
## Why it matters in finance
Clients can't easily check your work, so the whole industry runs on trust. A code of ethics tells the public what members promise to do.
A profession = specialized knowledge + a code of ethics + service to others. High ethical standards separate a profession from a trade group.
## Ethics vs law
Law is rule-based and the minimum. Ethics often asks for more: think about effects on others, not only what is legal.
## Traps
Overconfidence in your own morals; underestimating situational pressure; focusing on short-term results.
## Decision framework
Identify (facts, duties, conflicts) → Consider (options, people affected) → Decide and act → Reflect.
2: ## Code of Ethics (6 points)
1 Act with integrity, competence, diligence, respect.
2 Put the profession's integrity and clients' interests above your own.
3 Use reasonable care and independent judgment.
4 Act professionally and encourage others to do so.
5 Promote integrity and viability of capital markets.
6 Maintain and improve your competence.
## Standards (7 groups)
I Professionalism · II Capital markets · III Clients · IV Employers · V Analysis & recommendations · VI Conflicts · VII Member/candidate duties
Tip: memorize the group titles first, then the sub-standards inside each (next module).
3: ## I Professionalism
I(A) Follow the STRICTER of law vs Code. If others violate, dissociate (don't just report and stay).
I(B) Keep independence: modest gifts OK; client gifts disclosed to employer; issuer-paid research only for a flat fee.
I(C) No misrepresentation or plagiarism. I(D) No dishonesty/fraud. I(E) Stay competent.
## II Capital markets
II(A) Don't act on material nonpublic info. Mosaic theory: public + non-material private info = OK.
II(B) No price or volume manipulation (fake rumors, wash trades).
## III Clients

III(A) Loyalty, prudence, care (for a pension: owed to beneficiaries). III(B) Fair dealing: all clients get a fair chance. III(C) Suitability: know the client, follow the IPS. III(D) Fair, complete performance presentation. III(E) Keep client info confidential unless illegal activity or law requires.
## IV Employers

IV(A) Loyalty; can prepare a competing business but not solicit clients or take records while employed. IV(B) Outside compensation needs written consent from all parties. IV(C) Supervisors must make reasonable efforts to prevent violations.
## V Analysis
V(A) Diligence and reasonable basis. V(B) Communicate process, risks; separate fact from opinion. V(C) Keep records (7 years if no rule).
## VI Conflicts
VI(A) Disclose conflicts. VI(B) Priority: clients → employer → personal. VI(C) Disclose referral fees before the client signs.
## VII Member duties
VII(A) Don't cheat or reveal exam content. VII(B) 'CFA' is an adjective; no 'CFA Level II'.
4: ## Why GIPS
Global standards so managers present performance fairly and comparably. Stops cherry-picking best accounts.
## Who complies
Firms (and asset owners), firm-wide. Not individuals, not software.
## Composites
A composite groups ALL actual, fee-paying, discretionary portfolios with similar strategy. You can't leave out the losers.
## Verification
Optional. Done by an independent third party on a firm-wide basis.
5: ## How to answer ethics cases
1 Find who is owed a duty (client, employer, market).
2 Match the action to a standard (MNPI? fair dealing? conflict?).
3 Ask: was it disclosed? was consent written? was the client harmed or treated unfairly?
## Classic patterns
Trading on a tip about a deal → II(A). Giving the IPO only to big clients → III(B). Hidden bonus for selling in-house funds → VI(A) + III(C). Copying research → I(C).

1: ## Revenue and profit
Perfect competition: P = MR (flat demand). Others: MR < P.
Profit max: MR = MC (and MC not falling).
Economic profit counts opportunity costs; accounting profit doesn't.
## Breakeven and shutdown
Breakeven: P = ATC. Short-run shutdown: P < AVC. Long-run exit: P < ATC.
## Scale
Economies of scale: LRATC falls as output rises (specialization, bargaining). Diseconomies: rises (bureaucracy). Minimum efficient scale = lowest LRATC point.
## Four structures
Perfect competition → monopolistic competition → oligopoly → monopoly: fewer firms, more differentiation, pricing power and barriers.
Oligopoly = strategic behavior: kinked demand, Cournot, Stackelberg, Nash, price wars.
## Concentration
= HHI = Σ (share %)²; 4 firms × 25% = 2,500
Concentration ratio is simpler; neither captures barriers to entry.
2: ## Cycle types
Classical (level of GDP), growth cycle (vs trend), growth rate cycle (GDP growth rate).
## Four phases
Recovery (trough) → Expansion (above trend, boom) → Slowdown (biggest output gap, growth slowing) → Contraction (below potential).
## Credit cycles
Credit availability and price move in cycles. Strong credit peaks often precede banking crises.
## Indicators
Leading (before economy), coincident (with), lagging (after). Diffusion index = how widespread a move is.
3: ## Fiscal vs monetary
Fiscal = government taxes and spending. Monetary = central bank money and credit. Shared goal: stable growth, low stable inflation.
## Tools
Spending: transfers, current, capital. Taxes: direct (income), indirect (sales).
## Stance
Use the structural (cyclically adjusted) deficit, not the actual one, to judge if policy is expansionary.
Expansionary: cut taxes / raise spending. Contractionary: opposite.
Problems: lags, uncertain data, crowding out.
4: ## Central bank roles
Sole currency issuer, bank to government and banks, lender of last resort, payments supervisor, monetary policy, bank supervision.
## Tools
Policy rate (and repo), open market operations, reserve requirements.
## Transmission
Policy rate → short rates, asset prices, exchange rate, expectations → spending and inflation.
Effective inflation targeting needs independence, credibility, transparency. Many emerging markets target the exchange rate instead.
## Limits
Can't control how much people deposit or banks lend; liquidity trap at near-zero rates.
Ricardian equivalence: tax cuts may not boost spending if people expect future taxes.
5: ## Geopolitics
How geography affects politics and international relations. Actors cooperate or compete based on national interest.
Globalization: more trade and capital flows. Nationalism: less cooperation.
## Institutions
IMF: stability of the international monetary system. World Bank: fight poverty, development. WTO: global trade rules.
## Four archetypes
Autarky (self-sufficient), hegemony (dominant power), multilateralism, bilateralism.
## Tools
National security (alliances, conflict), economic (trade deals, nationalization), financial (currency access, foreign investment limits).
## Risk types
Event (scheduled, e.g., referendum), exogenous (sudden), thematic (evolving: climate, cyber).
Assess likelihood, velocity, size of impact; use scenarios and signposts.
6: ## Why trade
Specialization, scale economies, variety, competition, efficient allocation. Winners could compensate losers.
## Restrictions
Tariff = import tax → deadweight loss for the importing country.
Quota = quantity limit. VER = exporter limits itself. Export subsidy = paid per unit exported.
## Trading blocs (more integration →)
FTA (no internal tariffs) → customs union (+ common external tariff) → common market (+ free labor/capital) → economic union (+ common policies) → monetary union (+ one currency).
Trade creation: cheaper member imports replace domestic output. Trade diversion: costlier member imports replace cheaper outsiders.
7: ## FX basics
Largest market in the world. Real exchange rate = nominal rate adjusted for price levels (purchasing power).
= % change of base currency = new/old − 1 (quote as price/base)
## Regimes (fixed → floating)
Dollarization → currency board → fixed peg → target zone → crawling peg → managed float → free float.
## Capital controls
Used to stop capital flight in crises or limit hot-money inflows.

1: ## Business forms
Sole proprietorship and partnership: owners run it, unlimited liability, pass-through tax.
Limited company (corporation): separate legal entity, limited liability, owners ≠ managers, easy to transfer shares → easier to raise capital.
Private limited: ownership limits, often pass-through tax. Public limited: no ownership limits, may be double taxed, can list.
## Governance chain
Shareholders elect the board → board appoints managers. Shareholders change things by replacing directors.
## Public vs private
Public: liquid, transparent, more disclosure. Go public via IPO; go private via LBO.
2: ## Debt vs equity
Debt: fixed term, promised payments, priority claim. Equity: permanent, residual claim, unlimited upside.
Issuer view: debt is riskier (must pay). Investor view: equity is riskier.
Conflict: shareholders like risk (upside); debtholders dislike it (capped upside).
## Stakeholders
Shareholders, creditors, board, managers, employees, customers, suppliers, governments, society, environment.
Shareholder theory vs stakeholder theory (broader).
ESG factors can create risks and opportunities that affect value.
3: ## Principal–agent
Principal hires an agent; agent knows more and may act for itself.
Shareholders → directors → managers.
## Mechanisms
Financial reporting, shareholder meetings and votes, executive pay design, debt covenants, board independence and committees.
## Payoff
Weak governance → competitive disadvantage. Strong governance → efficiency, better controls, better performance.
4: ## Cash conversion cycle
= CCC = DOH + DSO − DPO
Shorter is better: collect faster, pay slower, hold less inventory.
Long CCC ↔ high net working capital / sales.
## Liquidity
Primary sources: cash, short-term investments, operating cash flow, credit lines.
Secondary (costly, crisis): issue equity, renegotiate, sell assets, bankruptcy protection.
Drags reduce inflows (bad receivables, obsolete stock). Pulls speed up outflows (suppliers want faster pay, credit cut).
## Approaches
Conservative: lots of working capital, long-term funding. Aggressive: little working capital, short-term funding.
5: ## Project types
Going concern (maintain), regulatory/compliance, expansion, other.
## Tools
NPV = PV inflows − PV outflows; accept if > 0. Measures value added.
IRR = rate where NPV = 0; accept if > hurdle. Conflicts with NPV for mutually exclusive projects → use NPV.
ROIC = company-wide return; compare with required return.
## Principles
After-tax cash flows, ignore sunk costs and financing costs, include effects on the rest of the firm (cannibalization, savings).
## Real options
Timing, abandonment, expansion, flexibility. Value = NPV without option + option value − option cost.
6: ## WACC
= WACC = wd·rd(1 − t) + wp·rp + we·re
Use market-value or target weights. Targets often stated as debt/EBITDA or a credit rating.
## Drivers
Business model (capital-light vs heavy), life cycle stage, revenue stability, operating leverage, market conditions.
## Modigliani–Miller
No taxes: capital structure doesn't affect value; re rises with leverage, WACC flat.
= MM II: re = r0 + (r0 − rd)(D/E)
With taxes: VL = VU + tD (tax shield).
## Real-world theories
Static trade-off: add debt until tax benefit = distress costs.
Pecking order: internal funds → private debt → public debt → equity last.

Who (customers), what (offer and value proposition), where (channels), how much (pricing).
Value proposition: why customers pick you. Value chain: how you create it.
Conventional models vs innovative ones (often digital: platforms, subscriptions, marketplaces).

Form expectations about future performance, position and risk for investment and credit decisions.

## Standards
IFRS (IASB) and US GAAP (FASB). Mostly converged but still differ in places.
2: ## Revenue: 5 steps
Contract → performance obligations → transaction price → allocate → recognize when each obligation is satisfied.
## Expenses
Match to revenue (COGS), to the period (admin), or over the benefit period (depreciation).
Choices and estimates (depreciation method, bad debts, warranties, useful life) change reported income.
## Non-recurring items
Discontinued operations shown separately, net of tax. Separate what will continue from what won't.
## EPS
= Basic EPS = (NI − preferred dividends) / weighted avg shares
Diluted: convertibles → if-converted; options → treasury stock (only if dilutive). Diluted ≤ basic.
Common-size income statement: each line ÷ revenue.
3: ## Measurement
Some items at fair value, some at historical/amortized cost.
## Intangibles
Finite life: amortize + impairment tests. Indefinite life: no amortization, test yearly.
IFRS: research expensed; development may be capitalized if criteria met.
Goodwill (from acquisitions): never amortized, tested for impairment yearly.
## Financial instruments
Fair value through profit/loss, fair value through OCI, or amortized cost.
## Ratios
Common-size balance sheet: each item ÷ total assets.
Liquidity: current, quick, cash ratios. Solvency: debt-to-assets, debt-to-equity.
4: ## Three sections
Operating (CFO), investing (CFI), financing (CFF).
## Direct vs indirect (CFO only)
Direct: cash from customers, cash to suppliers…
Indirect: start with NI, add non-cash charges, subtract gains, adjust working capital.
↑ current operating assets → subtract. ↑ current operating liabilities → add.
## IFRS vs US GAAP
US GAAP: interest paid/received, dividends received = CFO; dividends paid = CFF.
IFRS: more choice (interest/dividends paid CFO or CFF; received CFO or CFI).

Issuer, maturity, principal, coupon rate and frequency, seniority, contingency provisions.

Credit quality depends on repayment source, seniority, collateral, and willingness to pay.
## Indenture
The legal contract. Affirmative covenants = must do (pay taxes, insure). Negative covenants = must not (extra liens, sell key assets).

Bullet: all principal at maturity. Amortizing: principal paid along the way (sinking funds, waterfalls).
Floaters (MRR + margin), index-linked (inflation), step-up coupons, zero-coupon.

Call: issuer can redeem early (bad for investor → higher yield).
Put: investor can sell back (good for investor → lower yield).

Domestic, foreign (foreign issuer, local market), Eurobond (outside the currency's home, lighter rules).

By issuer type, credit quality, and maturity.

Broad aggregate or narrow (sector, rating, maturity). Used to benchmark and for index funds.

Companies: bank loans, commercial paper (unsecured note).

Investment grade: yield mostly benchmark rate. High yield: bigger issuer-specific spread, more covenants.

Can tax and print currency. Developed: stable. Emerging: faster growth, more volatile.

Forward (OTC, settle at end), futures (exchange, daily settlement), swaps (series of exchanges).

3: ## Portfolio approach
Diversification cuts risk without necessarily cutting return.
## Process
Planning (client needs, IPS) → Execution (asset allocation, security analysis, construction) → Feedback (monitor, rebalance, measure).
## Investors
Individuals; institutions: DB pensions, endowments, foundations, banks, insurers, sovereign wealth funds.
DC plan: employee bears risk. DB plan: sponsor bears risk.
## Industry
Active vs passive; traditional vs alternative managers. Trends: passive growth, big data, robo-advisers.
Products: mutual funds, SMAs, ETFs, hedge funds, PE/VC funds.
4: ## IPS
Written plan: objectives (risk and return) + constraints.
Constraints: liquidity, time horizon, legal/regulatory, tax, unique circumstances.
## Risk tolerance
Ability (objective: wealth, horizon, needs) + willingness (attitude). If they conflict, usually use the lower; educate if willingness is based on misunderstanding.
Objectives can be absolute (8% a year) or relative (beat an index).
## Asset allocation
Strategic asset allocation from asset classes with low correlation to each other.
## ESG approaches
Negative screening, positive screening, ESG integration, thematic, engagement, impact investing.
5: ## Two kinds of bias
Cognitive errors (faulty reasoning): easier to fix → moderate them.
Emotional biases (feelings): harder → often adapt to them.
## Belief perseverance (cognitive)
Conservatism, confirmation, representativeness, illusion of control, hindsight.
## Information processing (cognitive)
Anchoring, mental accounting, framing, availability.
## Emotional
Loss aversion, overconfidence, self-control, status quo, endowment, regret aversion.
## Market effects
Biases can help explain anomalies (momentum, bubbles, value effect).
6: ## Risk management
Not avoiding risk: choose risks deliberately, then measure, monitor and adjust to stay within tolerance.
## Framework
Governance → identification and measurement → infrastructure → policies → mitigation → communication → strategic integration.
Risk governance (board, risk committee, CRO) sets risk tolerance; enterprise-wide view.
Risk budgeting: allocate total risk across activities.
## Sources
Financial: market, credit, liquidity.
Non-financial: operational, legal, compliance, model, tax, settlement, solvency. Risks interact.
## Measure and modify
Measures: σ, β, duration, VaR, scenario/stress tests.
Modify: prevent/avoid, accept (self-insure), transfer (insurance), shift (derivatives).
